title: The ancestors
hook: God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob; many communities add Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah
carry: god of our fathers and mothers

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman at Shiloh whose lips moved without sound. Your line was hannah prayed quietly. Did you assume Hannah, not drunk, about someone? Today, the first blessing of the Amidah. Day five hundred seventy-seven.

How do you introduce yourself to someone important? Often, not with your own name. You lead with a connection. My grandmother used to talk about you. Your father helped mine when we first arrived. A name someone already trusts opens the door before yours does. The Amidah opens the same way. After the three steps, after open my lips, the first blessing doesn't say who the person praying is. It says whose family they come from.
screen: `HOW DO YOU INTRODUCE YOURSELF?` → `LEAD WITH A NAME THEY TRUST.` → `THE AMIDAH OPENS WITH FAMILY.`

segments.voice: The first blessing is called Avot: fathers, ancestors. It begins: blessed are You, our God and God of our fathers, God of Abraham, God of Isaac, and God of Jacob. That's straight from the burning bush. When Moses asks for God's name, God says, in the old Jewish translation, "The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Notice it doesn't say the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. It says God, three times. A Hasidic teaching, which tradition credits to the Baal Shem Tov, hears in that repetition that each one had to find God for himself; Isaac couldn't simply inherit Abraham's faith. The blessing goes on: the great, the mighty, the awesome God, words from Deuteronomy. Who remembers the kindness of the ancestors, and brings a redeemer to their children's children. It ends: blessed are You, shield of Abraham. People bow at its start and at its end. In recent decades, Reform, Conservative and Reconstructionist prayer books have offered the four mothers: Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah, so the line becomes God of our fathers and our mothers, and in some the ending names Sarah too. Orthodox communities keep the traditional words. Either way, the point of the blessing is the same: no one walks up to this prayer alone. You come carrying the people who brought you, and you ask to be heard partly because of them.
screen: `AVOT: GOD OF OUR FATHERS.` · `GOD OF ABRAHAM, GOD OF ISAAC...` · `EACH FOUND GOD FOR THEMSELVES.` · `SOME ADD SARAH, REBEKAH, RACHEL, LEAH.` · then, large: `GOD OF OUR FATHERS AND MOTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your own ancestors. Settle, and breathe. Start with the people who raised you. Say their names, in your head or under your breath. Then go back one more step, to their parents, if you know them. Then, if you can, one more. Where the names run out, notice that too: someone was there, and you don't know what to call them. With each name, think of one thing they handed down, a recipe, a stubbornness, a way of laughing. The bell holds the time.
Avot. Fathers, ancestors. The Amidah's first blessing, which comes before God by naming a family: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and in some communities Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah.
Your line: god of our fathers and mothers. Today, tell someone one story about one of your ancestors, even a small one. Day five hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Avot is the first blessing of every Amidah; people bend the knees and bow at its opening and closing words, and some non-Orthodox prayer books include the matriarchs Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Leah alongside the patriarchs.

original.note: Hebrew: fathers, ancestors. the name of the Amidah's first blessing.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of old names at the start of a prayer.
what it means: you come before God carrying your family; each ancestor found God for themselves.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 3:15 at the bush, Deuteronomy 10:17 for great, mighty and awesome; the imahot added in many non-Orthodox liturgies since the late twentieth century.
